nodes.label: Income Tax Act s.18D Deduction
nodes.rationale: NEW via Finance Bill 2026, conditional on assent. Deduction of the lower of 20% of total income or TT$20,000.

nodes.label: 50-70 Annuity Maturity Window
nodes.rationale: A new constraint from s.8(1)(ta), with direct planning consequences: an annuity maturing at 71 would NOT qualify for the exemption. Paired with the T&T residency condition.

nodes.label: Annuities: Insurance Act vs Securities Act Scope Gap
nodes.rationale: TOTAL GAP, not a negative finding. Item 10, flagged as most important, returned NOTHING: no TTSEC guidance, no Central Bank guidance, no commentary on whether BIR-approved deferred annuities fall within the Securities Act 2012 definition of 'security'. Evidential position: founder (CBTT-registered agent, 13+ yrs) says annuities are part of the life licence; consistent with Tatil's disclaimer and Round 2's finding that 'investment advice' attaches to securities; NO documentary corroboration found, and no contradiction either. Practitioner knowledge is the SOLE evidence — reasonable grounds to proceed, not grounds to stop asking. Confirm with counsel before launch. The volume of verified tax/NIS detail must not obscure that the highest-stakes question is unaddressed.
nodes.norm_label: annuities: insurance act vs securities act scope gap

nodes.label: Insurance Act 2018
nodes.rationale: The statute under which the founder's life licence is asserted to cover annuities. Named only as one side of the unresolved annuity-scope question; no documentary evidence located in this round.

nodes.label: eMoney Silent Modeling Error (Social Security understatement)
nodes.rationale: The named failure class: eMoney's Social Security setting understated a client's benefit until the client challenged it. The repo's stale 2008 PENSION_RATES is the same bug class in a worse direction — a systematic ~40% understatement on a suitability record the client signs.
nodes.norm_label: emoney silent modeling error (social security understatement)

nodes.label: Per-Parameter Provenance Rule
nodes.rationale: Every parameter needs its own source URL, retrieval date, and review date — PER-PARAMETER, NOT PER-PAGE. Proved by the NIBTT FAQ carrying one right constant (the $13,600 ceiling, current) and one wrong one (13.2%, stale) on the SAME page: a codebase trusting any single page wholesale will get some parameters right and others wrong, silently. Third independent proof alongside the government's stale TT$30k annuity page and the repo's 2008 rates; a fourth is the stale 2020 SCP form. Prefer the maintained page over the linked PDF.

nodes.label: Market Conduct Guideline (July 2023)
nodes.rationale: CONFIRMED. The Central Bank's Market Conduct Guideline (July 2023) imposes GENERIC Know-Your-Consumer, suitability, mis-selling-control and pre/during/post-sale disclosure duties — including modal premiums, fees and charges, and cash and surrender values. These map directly onto UL funding sustainability, in-force review, and illustration disclosure: nothing UL-specific is needed, the general duty already reaches it. The commission firewall and the anti-mis-selling term guardrail both exist to satisfy this Guideline. A suitability record affirmatively stating the recommendation was made without reference to commission is described as 'a Market Conduct gold standard'.

nodes.label: Convertible Level Term
nodes.rationale: Right for a TEMPORARY need with a known end date — income replacement while children are dependent, cover matching a mortgage term, protection to retirement. Cheapest cover per dollar. Tatil offers 10/15/20/25 yr and term-to-age 60/65/70. 1st-year commission 35% (vs whole life 60%). Premium ranking: term < whole life < endowment.

nodes.label: Convertibility
nodes.rationale: 🔥 'The killer feature'. Conversion to permanent needs NO MEDICAL EXAM and PRESERVES THE ORIGINAL HEALTH RATING FROM INCEPTION. So a healthy 30-year-old can buy cheap term now and lock the right to permanent cover later EVEN IF THEIR HEALTH DETERIORATES. A genuine planning lever — buy the option now, exercise it if life changes. No US tool localizes this to T&T products. Modelled as a product ATTRIBUTE in ProductCatalog. ⚠️ PARTIALLY UNVERIFIED: conversion WINDOWS are carrier-specific (US Guardian defaults to 5 years + an Extended Conversion Rider); the no-exam/preserved-rating mechanic is universal, THE WINDOW IS NOT. T&T carrier windows must be confirmed per product and come from ProductCatalog, never assumed. Listed under Open confirmations.

nodes.label: Whole Life
nodes.rationale: Right for a PERMANENT need — final expenses, an estate floor, a dependent who will never become independent, leaving a guaranteed sum. Lifelong cover + cash value. Premium and cash value are CONTRACTUAL; whole life CANNOT COLLAPSE from underfunding — that guarantee-vs-flexibility trade 'is the whole comparison' against UL. Pays the highest first-year commission at 60% (heaping schedule 60/15/10/5/5/2.5) — 120× a Platinum Edge policy — which is exactly why the commission firewall exists. REFUTED: 'whole life matures at 95/100' — a mischaracterization.

nodes.label: Limited-Pay Whole Life
nodes.rationale: Pay 10/15/20/25/30 yr, paid-up at 55/60/65. The design intent in one line: 'retire the PREMIUM before you retire the INCOME.' Right for someone who wants cover for life but no premiums in retirement.

nodes.label: Endowment
nodes.rationale: Right for a disciplined saver with a FIXED GOAL DATE — the canonical EDUCATION-FUNDING product (Sagicor Saver Series: 15/20/25 yr or to age 60/65/70; Tatil 15/20/25/30 yr). Pays sum assured on death during term, or an equal lump sum at maturity if you live. ⚠️ MOST EXPENSIVE of the three (term < whole life < endowment) because it must fund a guaranteed payout in a compressed window. This is WHY endowments fell from favour against 'buy term + invest the difference' — and exactly why an honest engine must SHOW that trade-off rather than sell the endowment.

nodes.label: Final Expense / Simplified Issue (Rest Assured)
nodes.rationale: Rest Assured (2024 product, terms to age 60/65/85/100), Peace Assured III. Right for the UNDERINSURED SENIOR — issue ages to 80, no medical, small face amounts for funeral/end-of-life. Fills a real gap for people other products decline.

nodes.label: Graded / Waiting Benefit
nodes.rationale: ⚠️ Simplified-issue products typically pay only PREMIUMS-PAID (not full face) on non-accidental death in the first ~12 months. Hard engine rule: NEVER present these as first-day full cover. Encoded as a load-bearing rule in RecommendationEngine's knowledge base.

nodes.label: Deferred Annuity 'Destiny' (fund-linked)
nodes.rationale: The retirement engine's CORE PRODUCT. Fund-linked: Option 1 Conservative, Options 2&3 Moderate/Aggressive. BIR-approved → shares the TT$60,000 aggregate deduction, and from 2026 the income exemption (50–70 maturity). Commission 5/3/1 + a '+0.25% Fund' TRAIL from years 3+ — a healthier incentive than pure heaping, aligning the agent with keeping the fund invested. OPEN: Destiny fund options imply investment risk BORNE BY THE CLIENT — confirm the annuity wrapper keeps fund selection inside the life licence and doesn't tip into securities advice.

nodes.label: Universal Life (Tatil Cashbuilder)
nodes.rationale: 'The only product in the catalog that can silently collapse. It needs its own rules.' UL UNBUNDLES an interest-credited accumulation account from a monthly cost-of-insurance deduction; credited rate is set AT THE INSURER'S DISCRETION above a contractual guaranteed minimum; surrender value = account balance − surrender charge. RIGHT FOR: irregular/commission-based income (skip a lean month, catch up in a good one), business owners, estate liquidity, someone who genuinely wants permanent cover WITH premium flexibility and will monitor it. WRONG FOR: anyone sold it as an 'investment' or 'savings plan' who actually needed term; MINIMUM-FUNDED UL (the classic time bomb — lapses in old age exactly when cover is irreplaceable); and any client who cannot or will not monitor it. ⚠️ PRODUCT-LEVEL DETAIL ENTIRELY UNVERIFIED for T&T: Tatil Cashbuilder, Sagicor and Guardian COI tables, crediting vs guaranteed minimum rates, surrender charge schedules, no-lapse guarantee availability, Option A/B availability — all sources are US/generic and citable FOR MECHANICS ONLY, never for a T&T contract. Must come from actual policy documents. CONFIRMED present in T&T: Pan-American Life T&T markets UL on flexible premiums, and CBTT capital adequacy regs name universal life as a distinct policy class.

nodes.label: Cost of Insurance (COI) & Net Amount at Risk
nodes.rationale: 'The whole product follows from one formula': COI charge = COI rate (rises with attained age) × Net Amount at Risk; Net Amount at Risk = death benefit − account value. THE CORE RISK, STATED PRECISELY: COI rates RISE with attained age while credited rates CAN BE CUT to the guaranteed floor. An underfunded policy's account value gets consumed from both ends — and the policy lapses or demands a large catch-up premium, AFTER DECADES OF PAYMENTS. Wisconsin's insurance regulator reports seeing this 'in many cases' among consumers who had paid for years. Mechanics citable from US/generic sources only.
nodes.norm_label: cost of insurance (coi) & net amount at risk

nodes.label: The Option A / Option B Trap
nodes.rationale: ⚠️ 'A real engine subtlety.' OPTION A / LEVEL: DB is fixed → extra funding raises account value → SHRINKS NAR → LOWERS COI; funding the policy well is genuinely protective. OPTION B / INCREASING: DB = face + account value → NAR STAYS PINNED AT FACE → extra funding does NOT reduce COI. So 'over-fund it to keep costs down' is TRUE under Option A and FALSE under Option B. The engine MUST know which option a policy carries before reasoning about its sustainability. ⚠️ Option A/B availability in T&T products is UNVERIFIED.
nodes.norm_label: the option a / option b trap

nodes.label: Illustration Risk / Vanishing Premium
nodes.rationale: 'Vanishing premium' is a DOCUMENTED MASS MIS-SELLING FAILURE, NOT AGENT ERROR. UL sold in high-interest eras on optimistic illustrations, promising premiums would stop; rates fell, policies didn't perform, premiums never vanished. General American settled for ~251,000 whole and universal life policyholders (1982–1996), US$55M. THE NAMED HAZARD: an illustration is a PROJECTION, NOT A PROMISE. Hard engine rule: never present an illustration as a promise. IN-FORCE ILLUSTRATIONS are the only way to know a UL is healthy — unlike whole life, a UL must be reviewed PERIODICALLY. Warning signs: declining account value, COI exceeding premium paid, a projected lapse age inside the client's life expectancy.

nodes.label: Policy X-ray → Legacy Cashbuilder Lapse Insight
nodes.source_location: Matching rules — Universal Life, 'the product insight this unlocks'
nodes.rationale: 🔥 'The product insight this unlocks': every legacy Cashbuilder the Policy X-ray finds on a client's book MAY BE HEADING FOR LAPSE RIGHT NOW, AND NOBODY KNOWS. A UL bought in the 1990s on 1990s crediting assumptions is exactly the failure profile. Flow: X-ray → flag every UL → request an in-force illustration → find the ones projected to lapse. A genuine service, a real review trigger, landing squarely on lapse prevention (#4). 'No US tool will ever do this for a Tatil Cashbuilder.'
nodes.norm_label: policy x-ray → legacy cashbuilder lapse insight

nodes.label: Group Life / Group Pension / Deposit Administration
nodes.rationale: 'The protection-gap engine.' Group life REDUCES 50% AT AGE 66 AND TERMINATES AT 70 — no post-retirement cover. Most employed clients are underinsured AND about to lose what they have. 'The single best prospecting insight for the individual-cover conversation: what you have through work vanishes exactly when you still have dependents.' Encoded in the gap formula: gap = need − (in-force individual cover + group cover, the latter ZEROED FROM 70). Also the 1–2× salary most employees have and lose on job change. Deposit Administration is a pooled employer retirement fund, tiered by fund size (≤30k / next 30k / >60k).
nodes.norm_label: group life / group pension / deposit administration

nodes.label: The Protection Gap
nodes.rationale: The organizing concept of the whole product: need − (in-force cover + group cover that will lapse at 70) = the gap the package fills. Also grounded in market data: T&T insurance penetration ~5.8% vs a ~7% global average; Caribbean life is a ~$3.4B market. 'Underinsurance is the market' — the product's job is to close that gap, not to fight for share of the already-insured.

nodes.label: Term Laddering & Packaging Principles
nodes.rationale: 'The right answer is usually a COMBINATION, matched to how obligations change over time.' TERM LADDER against declining obligation — stack a 25/20/15-yr layered so total cover STEPS DOWN as the mortgage amortizes and children age out. WHOLE LIFE FLOOR for the permanent piece (final expenses, the never-independent dependent). ANNUITY for the retirement need, maturity timed inside 50–70. CI/DISABILITY RIDER on the base policy for the health-shock need (cheaper attached than standalone). The per-debt years-to-payoff schedule from PALIG feeds the ladder's decline schedule — the spec previously asserted laddering against 'declining obligation' WITHOUT SAYING WHERE THE DECLINE SCHEDULE COMES FROM. It comes from PALIG.

nodes.label: The Core Suitability Principle (anti-mis-selling guardrail)
nodes.rationale: 'Selling expensive permanent cover when cheaper term would meet the need — WITHOUT DISCLOSING THE TERM OPTION — is a recognized mis-selling pattern.' The exact conflict the commission firewall exists to prevent (whole life pays 60% vs term's 35%). THE ENGINE'S RULE: when term satisfies the need, TERM MUST APPEAR among the three options WITH ITS LOWER COST SHOWN, even when a permanent product also fits. Omitting the cheaper option that works is the failure mode — and 'no silent truncation' already forbids it. Described in the spec as 'the client-side twin of the commission firewall'.

nodes.label: Plausible, Dated, and Wrong
nodes.rationale: Four plausible-sounding claims were REFUTED, 'and they're instructive because each is the kind of stale rule a naive build would ship': (1) 'annuity matures 50–75' — ceiling is 70, 50 is the statutory floor; (2) 'immediate annuity income exempt only if purchased on/after 1994 by a resident aged 60' — superseded by the 2026 exemption regime; (3) a per-product reading of the TT$60,000 cap — it is a single AGGREGATE ceiling; (4) 'whole life matures at 95/100' — a mischaracterization. 'The pattern is the same one this whole project keeps hitting: PLAUSIBLE, DATED, AND WRONG.' The knowledge base carries only verified rules, each with its refutation-tested provenance.

nodes.label: Ministry of the People, Social Development and Family Services
nodes.rationale: Publisher of the Senior Citizens' Pension schedule and application form. Its maintained page states the $5,500 income cap while its own linked 2020 application form still says $4,500 — a stale-document instance. Fetched via Firecrawl 2026-07-16.
nodes.norm_label: ministry of the people, social development and family services

nodes.label: SCP Means-Test Bands
nodes.rationale: CONFIRMED verbatim from the Ministry's own page, resolving the project's longest-running open question — and REVERSING a prior REFUTED 1-2 verification verdict. Maximum $3,500. Income <= 2,500 -> 3,500; 2,501-3,500 -> 2,500; 3,501-4,500 -> 1,500; 4,501-5,500 -> 500; > 5,500 -> 0 (hard disqualification). Age 65+. Residency: 20 years preceding application (absences <= 5 years total) OR 50 years aggregate. Banded, not pound-for-pound. The repo's bands match exactly. Caveat: rests on a single Ministry page and deserves a second source.

nodes.label: SCP Cliff Edges
nodes.rationale: $2,500 / $3,500 / $4,500 / $5,500 are hard thresholds, not tapers. At $5,501 of assessed income SCP goes to zero — one extra dollar costs $500/month. Design requirement: the engine must refuse to land a client just over a cliff without flagging it.

nodes.label: NIS Pension Counts as SCP Assessed Income
nodes.rationale: RESOLVED after surviving three research rounds unanswered. The official SCP application form settles it: item 6 requires 'Evidence of National Insurance Benefits / other Pension / Benefits'; item 31 asks 'Are you a Government or other pensioner? ... If so, how much is your monthly pension?'. The Ministry's eligibility clarification confirms the mechanism: an applicant 'in receipt of an alternative monthly income' did not meet income eligibility and was not approved. The founder was right; the repo was right. The one-time NIS grant is excluded (not monthly income) — by inference, not yet by statute.
nodes.norm_label: nis pension counts as scp assessed income

nodes.label: NIS-SCP Interaction (Clawback)
nodes.rationale: REAL and provable from two primary sources, after being wrongly DOWNGRADED to 'unverified hypothesis' by parameter-verification-2026-07.md. No NIS pension: $0 NIS + $3,500 SCP = $3,500. NIS minimum: $3,000 + $2,500 SCP = $5,500. So a $3,000 NIS pension delivers only $2,000 of additional income — a third is offset. Counter-intuitive corollary that survives: SCP's maximum ($3,500) EXCEEDS the NIS minimum pension ($3,000), so someone who never qualified for an NIS pension can receive more from SCP alone than a 750-contribution NIS retiree. NOTE: the 'modal outcome' framing depended on the stale 2008 table where every class fell below $3,000; under 2016 basics classes XIII-XVI clear it.

nodes.label: Senior Citizens' Pension Act Chap. 32:02
nodes.rationale: STILL OPEN. laws.gov.tt is DNS-blocked from this environment; Firecrawl reaches it but the /ttdll-web/revision/download/43781?type=act endpoint returns raw PDF bytes it doesn't parse. The Ministry's published schedule is sufficient to build on; the Act would add the statutory definition of 'income' and confirm whether the NIS grant is excluded by law rather than by inference. Confirmed NOT amended by Finance Bill 2026.

nodes.label: Stale SCP Application Form (2020, states $4,500)
nodes.rationale: The linked 2020 SCP application form states 'The person's income must not exceed $4,500.00 per month' while the Ministry's current page says $5,500 — the form is a revision behind. The same failure as the Ministry of Finance's TT$30,000 annuity page and NIBTT's 13.2% FAQ. Three government sources, three stale documents. Rule: source + date per parameter, and prefer the maintained page over the linked PDF.

nodes.label: Adversarial Verification Failure Pattern
nodes.rationale: Two confidently wrong verification results, both on things the founder's repo had right — though the record is itself contested. (1) SCP bands: REFUTED 1-2 and the interaction declared unverifiable; the Ministry's own page and application form prove otherwise; repo was correct. (2) NIS benefit rates: initially accused of fabricating a '2016 schedule' 3-0 — but that accusation was ITSELF false; the 2016 schedule exists at Contribution_Rates/Benefit_rates_retire_and_invalid_sep2016.html with exactly the reported figures and effective date, so the 3-0 verification was RIGHT and the repo IS stale. Both original errors ran the same direction: overriding a practitioner's domain knowledge with search-derived speculation. In each case the authoritative answer was on the issuing agency's own website the entire time. Rule: a unanimous or majority vote over search results is not evidence.

nodes.label: LifeSPAN (Critical Illness)
nodes.rationale: Tatil full critical illness plan: lump sum up to $2,000,000 on diagnosis, 23 covered critical illnesses, unrestricted use of proceeds. VERIFICATION STATUS: MARKETING PAGES ONLY — tatil.co.tt states 'Conditions Apply'; no product specification exists and the sample contract is pending. MUST NOT be encoded as engine rules; the engine must present the condition list as marketing-sourced and defer to policy wording. Chosen over Lite whenever the client can pass underwriting or needs cover above $250,000.

nodes.label: LifeSPAN Lite
nodes.rationale: Simplified-issue CI plan: only 4 major illnesses (Cancer, Heart Attack, Stroke, Coma), sum insured $75,000–$250,000, no medical exams, issue ages 20–50 (cover to 60) or 20–60 (cover to 70). Explicit 2-year waiting period during which only a refund of premiums is payable. Design intent / decision rule: Lite exists for clients who cannot pass underwriting, need speed, or for whom $250k suffices. No female benefit, no maternity benefit, no ROP mentioned. VERIFICATION STATUS: marketing pages only.

nodes.label: Female Benefit — automatic +25% coverage
nodes.rationale: Female insureds automatically receive an additional 25% on policy coverage if diagnosed with Breast Cancer, Cervical Cancer, Ovarian Cancer, or Cancer of the Uterus. Automatic, not an optional rider — a $500,000 policy pays $625,000 on breast cancer diagnosis. WHY IT MATTERS: a genuinely differentiated, sex-specific benefit that no US planning tool models; a 1.25x multiplier for a female insured on the four named cancers. It is the reason LifeSPAN strictly dominates LifeSPAN Lite for any female client whose concern is breast/gynaecological cancer. VERIFICATION STATUS: marketing-sourced ('Conditions Apply'); whether the uplift applies to in-situ diagnoses is unverified.

nodes.label: Breast Cancer
nodes.rationale: One of four named cancers attracting the automatic +25% female benefit, and the anchor use case for the whole LifeSPAN recommendation. Its value is threatened by the cancer definition gap: DCIS (ductal carcinoma in situ) is among the most common breast cancer diagnoses and is typically excluded by CI policies as carcinoma in situ.

nodes.label: Cancer Definition Gap (carcinoma in situ / DCIS)
nodes.rationale: UNVERIFIED and DECISIVE. Nearly all CI policies exclude carcinoma in situ and early-stage disease. DCIS is among the most common breast cancer diagnoses, so coverage may hinge entirely on staging language not yet seen. Described as the single most important unknown for the breast-cancer use case. Related unknowns from the same list: whether the +25% female benefit applies to in-situ diagnoses; survival period (most CI plans require 14–30 days post-diagnosis); accelerated vs additional (does the CI payout reduce the death benefit); LifeSPAN's own waiting period (page is silent, Lite states 2 years); pre-existing condition exclusions; severity tiering; issue ages, premium structure and commission (age-banded 35/30/25/20 for LifeSPAN, 30/15/2.5 for Lite). WHY: a client with DCIS discovering at claim time they were not covered is precisely the mis-selling failure the product exists to prevent.
nodes.norm_label: cancer definition gap (carcinoma in situ / dcis)

nodes.label: Maternity Benefit
nodes.rationale: After the policy has been in force 2 years, provides free first-year coverage on a $10,000 children's savings policy for a newborn. Maximum 2 children per female insured. LifeSPAN only — not offered on Lite. VERIFICATION STATUS: marketing-sourced.

nodes.label: Refund of Premium (ROP)
nodes.rationale: Optional benefit refunding all premiums paid net of policy fees, in three variants: ROP on death, ROP at maturity, ROP at either. DESIGN INTENT: reframes CI cover as 'your money back if you never claim' — a real objection-handler for clients who resist paying for something they may never use. Also exists as an ROP rider on the Whole Life 2023 spec. VERIFICATION STATUS: LifeSPAN ROP is marketing-sourced; the Whole Life 2023 ROP rider is spec-confirmed.

nodes.label: Total Disability Waiver of Premium
nodes.rationale: Optional rider waiving the basic premium during total disability. Appears on LifeSPAN (marketing-sourced) and as TDWP on Cashbuilder II (spec-confirmed).

nodes.label: Critical Illness Rider on Whole Life 2023
nodes.rationale: CONFIRMED from the Whole Life 2023 spec: a Critical Illness rider (entry 17, max entry 50/55/60 for plans maturing at 60/65/70) with an ROP rider refunding all premiums net of policy fees. STRUCTURAL CONSEQUENCE: CI is available both standalone (LifeSPAN) and as a rider on Whole Life — a real choice the engine must model, since riders are typically cheaper attached than standalone.
nodes.norm_label: critical illness rider on whole life 2023

nodes.label: Whole Life 2023
nodes.rationale: Tatil whole life product whose 2023 specification is authoritative and carries a Critical Illness rider plus an ROP rider. Also charges roughly 3% more for monthly mode, unlike Cashbuilder II which has no modal loading.

nodes.label: Universal Life
nodes.rationale: Product structure with a life insurance portion and a fund portion: premiums are paid into the fund, interest is calculated and compounded daily, the fund accumulates cash value, and the cost of the life insurance portion is paid out of that cash value. Cashbuilder II's own specification confirms the fund/COI separation the UL knowledge base describes.

nodes.label: Cashbuilder II (1992) — retail UL
nodes.rationale: AUTHORITATIVE — Tatil's own 1992 retail universal life specification. Minimum sum insured $10,000, no maximum, no age restriction, 'Age Next'. Maturity defaults to the greater of age 65 or 10 years from issue, overridable subject to a 10-year minimum. No female setback for minimum premium calculations. No modal loadings — the annual minimum is simply the monthly minimum x12, unlike every other Tatil product (WL/Endowment/Rest Assured charge ~3% more monthly), a real cross-product inconsistency. Medical ratings: Table B–D → +100% (x1.0), Table E–F → +150% (x1.5), Table H → +200% (x2.0); occupational/avocational flat extras convert to multipliers. Riders: AD (max 2x SI or global limit, expires 65, ages 15–60, $1.25/thousand), AD&D (max 2x SI or $150,000 whichever less, expires at anniversary preceding 60th birthday, $1.70/thousand — AD and AD&D mutually exclusive), TDWP, WPDDP, DIR. STILL UNVERIFIED: COI rate tables, Option A vs Option B classification, current credited rates, expense charges (in the 59-page spec, not yet extracted).

nodes.label: Cashbuilder III (1995) — corporate deferred compensation UL
nodes.rationale: AUTHORITATIVE — Tatil's own 1995 specification. A Universal type product closely resembling Cashbuilder II, structured as a deferred compensation plan subject to Section 134(6A) of the Income Tax Act. Employer-owned, on the life of the employee, for the employee's benefit; employer pays; each policy must be BIR-approved before issue. Cannot be borrowed against, assigned, or surrendered (BIR conditions for deductibility); deregistration may be applied for, after which surrender is possible for accumulated value less tax and charges. Death benefit = sum insured + net accumulation (if positive). Min SI $10,000, no max; issue ages 18–55. Maturity normally 65, ages 51–70 considered; income may commence not earlier than 50 and not later than 70 — the 50–70 window appearing already in a 1995 document. Grace 30 days. Planned premium must be paid in year 1; thereafter the accumulation must be positive to keep the policy in force. Minimum monthly premium $100 (spec) vs $250 (brochure) — an unresolved discrepancy — with a full age x sum-insured minimum-premium grid (18–30/31–40/41–50/51–55 x $10k–$950k bands). Retirement options: (a) full pension on fund balance, (b) 25% tax-free cash lump sum + reduced pension on 75%, (c) guarantee period 5/10/15 years. At resignation likely surrendered subject to BIR approval. Death before retirement: sum insured + fund balance paid to the employer for the beneficiary's benefit, as lump sum or annuity on survivor's life. Expense charges stated as identical to Cashbuilder II.
nodes.norm_label: cashbuilder iii (1995) — corporate deferred compensation ul

nodes.label: Premium Vacation
nodes.rationale: Tatil's own marketing term, from the Cashbuilder II spec: at certain points a policy owner may take a 'premium vacation' and let the cash value pay the expenses of the policy, so the life insurance remains in force even though no premiums are being paid. TRADE-OFF — this is the lapse mechanic named in the vendor's own language: it is simultaneously the flexibility that makes UL right for irregular income AND the exact feature that silently kills underfunded policies decades later, once COI has risen with attained age. AUTHORITATIVE (Tatil spec).

nodes.label: Minimum Monthly Premium (MMP)
nodes.rationale: The minimum monthly amount which will provide coverage for ten years and allow for a positive Accumulation after the policy has been in force for two years. DESIGN INTENT: MMP is the anti-collapse floor, defined at issue — the structural counterweight to the premium vacation mechanic. Related: PPP (Planned Periodic Payment) is what the owner agreed to pay; it must be >= MMP and be paid every mode for the first two years. AUTHORITATIVE (Cashbuilder II spec).

nodes.label: Technically Lapsed (commission clawback state)
nodes.rationale: A named policy state in the Cashbuilder II commission mechanics: 'If a policy was previously lapsed or technically lapsed in the first year all projected commissions would have been clawed back.' Sits inside an unusual commission structure — commissions are advanced then worked down by actual premiums, while lump sums pay 'as-earned', do not work down the advance, and are commissionable at a reduced rate. WHY IT MATTERS: this chargeback mechanic makes lapse prevention the agent's economic self-interest, not merely good service. AUTHORITATIVE (Tatil spec).

nodes.label: Section 134(6A) Income Tax Act — corporate deferred compensation
nodes.rationale: The Trinidad & Tobago corporate deferred-compensation regime governing Cashbuilder III. Resolves a prior open question: this is what s.134(6) is for — the section that appeared in the tax research with no explanation. Conditions for deductibility (per BIR): employer-owned policy on the employee's life, each policy BIR-approved before issue, and the policy cannot be borrowed against, assigned, or surrendered unless deregistration is granted. AUTHORITATIVE as to the regime's existence and role; the specific one-third limit is UNVERIFIED.
nodes.norm_label: section 134(6a) income tax act — corporate deferred compensation

nodes.label: One-Third of Income Rule (s.134(6A))
nodes.rationale: UNVERIFIED — 1995 DOCUMENT. The Cashbuilder III literature states 'the maximum premium is one-third of the chargeable income of the employee' and that the entire premium including lump sums is eligible for tax relief, which together with other tax savings plans must not exceed 1/3 of assessable income. This is NOT the TT$60,000 combined cap (s.28(15)); s.134(6A) deferred compensation appears to run on a one-third-of-income limit instead. CAUTION: whether the 1/3 rule survives, and how it interacts with the modern TT$60,000 cap, is unverified and must not be assumed. It is a strong lead: if s.134(6A) really allows one-third of income, it is a far larger allowance for high earners than $60k, and the engine's envelope optimizer would be materially wrong to ignore it.

nodes.label: Illustration Risk Smoking Gun (CBIII 10.5% vs 4% guarantee)
nodes.rationale: The vanishing-premium scenario documented in the product's own literature. Cashbuilder III was sold in 1994/95 crediting 10.5% against a guaranteed rate of 4%, with the framing 'substantially higher rates have been credited to similar plans over the past five years' — the exact optimistic-illustration language that produced the General American settlement (~251,000 policyholders, US$55M). The collapse mechanic is explicit: 'thereafter, the accumulation must be positive to keep the policy in force.' CONSEQUENCE: a CBIII written in 1995 on a 10.5% assumption, now crediting nearer its 4% floor, with COI rising every year on a life ~30 years older, is a textbook candidate for silent collapse. This makes Cashbuilder the Policy X-ray's highest-value target — find every Cashbuilder on a client's book, request an in-force illustration, identify the ones projected to lapse. Real service, real review trigger, and something no US tool will ever do for a Tatil Cashbuilder. The rate quotes are AUTHORITATIVE (Tatil spec); current credited rates are UNVERIFIED.
nodes.norm_label: illustration risk smoking gun (cbiii 10.5% vs 4% guarantee)

nodes.label: Option A vs Option B Gap (level vs increasing death benefit)
nodes.rationale: UNVERIFIED — NEEDS CONFIRMATION. Cashbuilder II states death benefit = sum insured + net accumulation, which resembles Option B (fund on top of face) rather than Option A (level). If so, extra funding does NOT reduce COI — the trap identified in the UL knowledge base. The specs describe the mechanic but publish no COI rate tables, so this cannot be settled from the documents in hand.
nodes.norm_label: option a vs option b gap (level vs increasing death benefit)

nodes.label: Disability Income Rider (DIR)
nodes.rationale: Cashbuilder II rider paying $1,000/month per $100,000 sum insured; issue ages 20–55; expires at 60; 6-month elimination period. AUTHORITATIVE (Tatil spec).

nodes.label: Waiver of Premium on Death/Disability of Payor (WPDDP)
nodes.rationale: Cashbuilder II rider waiving premiums on the death or disability of the payor — designed for policies where someone other than the insured pays, e.g. a parent funding a child's policy. AUTHORITATIVE (Tatil spec).
nodes.norm_label: waiver of premium on death/disability of payor (wpddp)

It also hypothesised the silent-collapse scenario that the CBIII spec's ingredients confirm, and it named the Option B extra-funding trap that the CBII death benefit definition may trigger.
